prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how gains from trade operate through reallocation across firms.

statement.case_for: The Melitz (2003) selection model, together with Helpman's wider programme on firm-level trade (including exports versus FDI with Melitz and Yeaple), moved the unit of analysis in trade from countries and sectors to firms. It showed that gains from trade and the effects of liberalisation run through reallocation within industries. That produced a durable link between theory and large firm-level microdata, and it is now standard in teaching, empirical work and policy models. More than two decades of testing and extension mean maturity is not a concern. The work also fits a criterion I weigh heavily: it changed what economists measure and how they know it, by tying a tractable model to new micro evidence. This is a judgement from general knowledge, not from independent verification. After reading colleagues' openings I keep this as my preferred single-achievement configuration, with two credited names that match the clearest anchors of the contribution.
statement.case_against: The credited set omits several co-originators of the firm-level trade literature, notably Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, so any allocation of credit here is open to challenge. Trade was recognised in 2008 through Krugman, and some colleagues may see the field as already covered or may prefer a quantitative-trade basis. B040 has much broader opening support. It also has a cleaner two-person attribution in Kiyotaki and Moore (1997), because no obvious co-originators are missing from its credited set. The empirical magnitudes of the gains from trade under heterogeneous firms are still debated.

responses.point: Ranked B036 eighth. He sees overlap with other trade candidates, which could split credit, and asks whether Melitz is sufficiently distinct from the earlier recognition of trade theory through Krugman.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously for attribution. Within the shortlist, though, B036 is the only trade candidate, so the splitting concern bears on how the credited names should be chosen and not on whether the discovery is prize-worthy. On distinctness, Krugman's prize concerned scale economies and trade patterns at the country and industry level. Melitz and Helpman changed the unit of analysis to the firm and identified a reallocation channel that can be tested with micro data. I think that is a different discovery, not an extension of the earlier one. I agree the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is the real weakness, and I have limited the proposal to the two clearest anchors.

responses.point: Ranked B002 first. He argues that population-scale administrative data changed the measurement of mobility and showed that childhood place matters causally, and he proposes Chetty and Hendren as the cleanest core.
responses.response: I value this kind of data-building and agree the measurement advance is substantial. I rank it lower on maturity and attribution. The central results date from about 2014 onward, and he himself notes that the long-run durability of the neighbourhood-effect estimates is still being tested. Credit within a large collaborative programme is hard to draw at two or three names. By contrast, the heterogeneous-firm framework has two decades of replication and refinement behind it. This is a difference of timing and boundary rather than of quality, and I would revisit it if the committee judges the causal evidence settled enough.

responses.point: Ranked B040 first. He argues that Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the clear originating contribution on collateral constraints, that a two-person award is cleanest, and that overlap with the 2022 prize is the main risk.
responses.response: I agree his attribution is cleaner than mine, since no obvious co-originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism are missing from the credited set. That is a real advantage over B036. I do not see the 2022 overlap as decisive, since the mechanism is distinct from the bank-run and crisis analysis recognised then. My reservation is the empirical side. He and others note that direct validation of the amplification mechanism is more mixed than its theoretical influence suggests. I rank it second and name it as my first alternative, and I would not oppose it if the committee weighs clean attribution above empirical grounding.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-name credit that leaves out Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, or whether the omitted co-originators make the trade award unsafe.
Whether Redding should be added as a third name for the quantitative extensions, as one colleague proposes. I currently treat him as a later extender.
How much the 2008 prize to Krugman should reduce the marginal case for another trade award.
Whether the empirical support for the reallocation channel's welfare implications is strong enough given the quantitative-trade debate.
My assessment relies on general knowledge, not independent verification of citations or impact.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in economic history, with no listed co-authorship or institutional tie to the credited trade names. Lund colleagues on the committee are not connected to this candidate in the profile.
